row.note: The commentary contrasts the guided path of the favored with loss; this verse says YHWH knows the righteous way while the wicked way perishes, giving the same moral contrast an explicit outcome.
The commentary distinguishes a route that reaches a destination from dalal as disappearance without one; Jesus places the many on a broad road ending in destruction.
The commentary's sirat is a traversed way with an arrival; this verse makes the difficult way lead to life.
The commentary sets the way of those graced against the lost; the Community Rule divides people between ways of light and darkness with opposed ends, showing a Second Temple Jewish two-ways frame.

row.basis: way of life and way of death
row.note: The commentary's two forms of going are set against each other; the Didache opens by naming two ways and says their difference is great.
The commentary presents dalal as a way whose destination is lost; the Didache specifies the way of death through the conduct that marks it.
The commentary's sirat is called straight; Isaiah describes the righteous person's path as level, making rectitude a property of the route itself.
The commentary asks for a way that carries travelers to an end; Isaiah's highway is for the redeemed returning to Zion, and fools do not stray on it.
The commentary identifies a path with a direction and destination; Jeremiah tells the people to seek the good way, walk in it, and find rest.

row.basis: voice says which way to walk
row.note: The commentary's prayer is for guidance on the path; Isaiah depicts a voice directing a traveler, “This is the way, walk in it.”
The commentary's sirat is a route toward an arrival; the psalmist asks God to make known the way he should go.
The commentary joins guidance with a straight road; the psalm asks God's good spirit to lead the speaker on level ground.
The commentary asks to be guided along a path; the psalmist asks God to make his ways known.
The commentary's path is a route under divine direction; the psalmist asks God to lead and teach him.
The commentary identifies the sirat as a directed road; the shepherd leads the speaker in paths of righteousness.
The commentary calls the requested sirat straight; Proverbs says trust in YHWH and he will make one's paths straight.

row.basis: deliberate route around the nearer road
row.note: The commentary says a road can carry a traveler to an end even while he leaves sight; God declines the nearer Philistine road because of the people's vulnerability and chooses a route toward the sea.
The commentary's road has a direction and arrival; Israel is led around through the wilderness toward the sea, so guidance need not mean the shortest route.

row.basis: guarded way to a prepared place
row.note: The commentary describes a traveler disappearing along a road that still has a destination; God sends a messenger to guard Israel on the way and bring them to the prepared place.

row.basis: God goes ahead to find a campsite
row.note: The commentary's route has a direction and endpoint; Moses recalls God going before Israel to find where they should camp.

row.basis: led on the journey to a household
row.note: The commentary's sirat has an arrival; Abraham's servant says God led him on the way to his master's kin.

row.basis: blind led on an unknown way
row.note: The commentary's blind people strive toward the path yet cannot see it; Isaiah promises that God will lead blind people on an unfamiliar way, turn darkness to light, and not abandon them.

row.basis: blind groping and failing on the way
row.note: The commentary's scene has people unable to see the path; Deuteronomy pictures the blind groping in darkness and failing in their ways.
The commentary's blind runners cannot see the path; Isaiah depicts people groping like the blind and stumbling even at noon.
The commentary places blindness beside a path that cannot be seen; Jesus' image has a blind guide and blind follower both falling into a pit.
The commentary's scene concerns people blinded as they try to reach a path; Elisha's pursuers are struck blind, making this a concrete biblical scene of divinely imposed blindness.
The commentary's lost sight leaves people unable to find their way; after the blinding in the neighboring verse, Elisha leads the soldiers to Samaria, where their eyes are opened.

row.basis: lost in wilderness without a city
row.note: The commentary says dalal can mean going where no one knows where the person went; these travelers wander in a desert way and cannot find a city to settle in.

row.basis: straight way to an inhabited city
row.note: The commentary contrasts directionless loss with a route that arrives; God leads the lost travelers by a straight way to a city.
The commentary's lost person has gone where no one knows; Ezekiel pictures God searching for scattered sheep and rescuing them from the places where they were dispersed.

row.basis: lost sheep found in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary uses dalal for someone whose whereabouts are unknown; Jesus' shepherd searches the wilderness until he finds the lost sheep.

row.basis: Joseph hidden in the dry pit
row.note: The commentary recalls Joseph disappearing into the pit before reaching a caravan; Genesis tells the same scene, with the pit empty of water.

row.basis: pulled from the pit into the traders' route
row.note: The commentary says Joseph's disappearance in the pit leads to the road and travelers; Genesis has passing traders draw him up and carry him into their journey.

row.basis: Joseph interprets his journey as being sent ahead
row.note: The commentary reads the pit's disappearance as a route with an eventual destination; Joseph later says God sent him ahead to preserve life, interpreting that route as purposeful.

row.basis: Joseph sold, yet God was with him
row.note: The commentary's Joseph vanishes from his brothers and passes into travelers' hands; Stephen retells the sale to Egypt while stressing that God was with Joseph.

row.basis: pit containing no water but danger
row.note: The commentary treats the pit as Joseph's hiding place before the caravan route; Genesis Rabbah reads its emptiness of water as leaving snakes and scorpions, heightening the apparent finality from which Joseph emerges.
The commentary explains dalal with burial and disappearance into earth; Genesis says the human returns to dust, giving the image its deathly endpoint.
The commentary quotes those who ask whether people lost in earth can be created anew; Isaiah directly addresses the dead in dust and calls them to awake.
The commentary's earth-hidden dead are asked whether they can be newly created; Daniel pictures sleepers in the dust of the earth awakening.
The commentary's dalal includes the dead buried and lost in earth; Ezekiel's vision promises that God will open graves and bring the dead up.
The commentary presents the question of new creation after bodies disappear into earth; Job asks whether a dead person will live again, preserving the question in a different voice.

row.basis: God calls and the dead answer
row.note: The commentary connects disappearance in earth with eventual meeting; Job imagines God calling and the dead answering, giving the hoped-for return a personal encounter.
The commentary reports the objection that the dead lost in earth cannot be newly created; the martyr answers that the King of the universe will raise the dead to renewed life.
The commentary's earth-disappearance question concerns whether the dead can be made new; Paul describes what is sown perishable being raised imperishable.

row.basis: the dead hear and come out
row.note: The commentary's dead are hidden in earth; Jesus says all in the tombs will hear his voice.
The commentary's question concerns the destination after bodily disappearance; John distinguishes those who come out to life from those who come out to judgment.
The commentary's people lost in earth ask about new creation; Paul says the dead in Christ rise at the Lord's descent.
The commentary's reply to disappearance is framed as meeting the Lord; Paul says the living and resurrected will be caught up to meet him.

row.basis: earth gives up those asleep in it
row.note: The commentary's dalal includes burial in earth; 4 Ezra pictures the earth restoring those who sleep in it at the judgment.
The commentary's question is whether the body lost in earth can be created again; 2 Baruch says the earth will restore the dead it now receives.

The commentary presents resurrection as the answer to bodies disappearing into earth; the Talmud's debate derives resurrection from Torah, showing how Jewish interpretation makes that answer scriptural.
The commentary says the things idolaters fabricated disappear from them; Moses asks where the nations' gods are when their worshippers need refuge.

row.basis: idol makers and witnesses are nothing
row.note: The commentary says fabricated objects vanish at the gathering; Isaiah calls the makers of idols nothing and their witnesses unable to see or know.

row.basis: idol worshippers cannot see or understand
row.note: The commentary depicts fabricated objects disappearing from their adherents; Isaiah says the idol-makers' eyes are shut and their hearts cannot understand.
The commentary says the objects people invented leave them; Jeremiah exposes the image as a lie with no breath in it.
The commentary places the loss of fabricated objects at judgment; Jeremiah says they perish when the time of their punishment comes.
The commentary says the objects on which people relied disappear; the psalm describes their mouths and eyes as useless, exposing the absence of a responding power.
The commentary says the fabrications leave their worshippers; the psalm adds that those who make and trust them become like them, sharing their incapacity.
The commentary says fabricated things disappear from their makers; Wisdom says human inventions become abominations and traps for souls, spelling out the spiritual harm of that reliance.
The commentary says no one is absent from the Day of Judgment; Amos says that digging into Sheol will not hide people from God's hand.
The commentary denies disappearance from judgment; Amos names the mountain's summit as another place God will search.
The commentary says none can be absent from judgment; Amos says even captives among enemies remain within God's reach.
The commentary says no one can be absent from the Day of Judgment; Job says God's eyes are on human ways and steps.
The commentary denies that anyone can vanish from judgment; Job says evildoers have no darkness or deep shadow where they can hide.
The commentary says people cannot disappear from the judgment day; the psalm asks where one could flee from God's spirit or presence.
The commentary says no one is absent from judgment; the psalm says night is as bright as day to God, so darkness cannot hide a person.
The commentary says none are absent on the Day of Judgment; Daniel sees the court sit and books opened, giving judgment an image of complete accounting.
The commentary denies disappearance from the judgment day; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, including what is hidden, into judgment.

row.basis: the dead stand before the throne
row.note: The commentary says no one is absent from the Day of Judgment; Revelation pictures the dead, great and small, standing before the throne as books are opened.

row.basis: all stand before God's judgment seat
row.note: The commentary denies anyone can be absent from judgment; Paul says all will stand before God's judgment seat.
The commentary says no one escapes the Day of Judgment; Paul specifies that each person will give an account to God.
The commentary says the Lord neither loses nor forgets; Isaiah contrasts a mother who might forget with God's assurance that Zion will not be forgotten.
The commentary says God's knowledge of past generations is kept in a book; Malachi describes a book of remembrance written before God for those who fear him.
The commentary says nothing is lost from God's knowledge; the psalm asks God to keep the speaker's tears in a bottle and record them in a book.
The commentary says the Lord does not lose or forget; Jesus says not one sparrow is forgotten before God.
The commentary says God's knowledge is preserved rather than lost; Avot teaches that all deeds are written in a book, an ethical interpretation of divine accounting.
The commentary joins God's complete knowledge to the Day of Judgment; the rabbinic account of books opened on Rosh Hashanah turns remembrance into a judgment record.
The commentary says the Lord does not lose the history of earlier generations; Exodus says God heard Israel's groaning and remembered the covenant with the patriarchs.

row.basis: traveler asks for safe guidance and arrival
row.note: The commentary's sirat is a traveler's road with an endpoint; the traveler's prayer asks God to lead the journey in peace and bring the traveler safely to the intended destination.

row.basis: strayed from the way of truth
row.note: The commentary contrasts a way that reaches its destination with dalal as losing the way; at judgment Wisdom's speakers confess that they strayed from the way of truth and lacked righteousness's light.
The commentary says the lost person has gone where no one knows; Wisdom's speakers say they journeyed through trackless deserts and did not know the Lord's way.

row.basis: fool cannot find the way to the city
row.note: The commentary explains dalal as someone going where no one knows where; Ecclesiastes says the fool does not know the way to the city, making loss a failure to reach a concrete destination.

row.basis: leaders wander in a pathless waste
row.note: The commentary contrasts a guided road with directionless disappearance; Job says God makes the leaders of the people wander in a trackless waste.
The commentary's blinded people cannot see the path; Job pictures leaders groping in darkness without light and staggering like a drunk.
The commentary's sirat is a straight way with an arrival; Proverbs depicts the righteous path as light growing toward full day.

row.basis: way of the wicked is darkness
row.note: The commentary distinguishes an arriving path from losing one's way; Proverbs says the wicked walk in darkness and do not know what makes them stumble.
The commentary contrasts the straight sirat with dalal; Proverbs depicts people leaving straight paths to walk in darkness.
The commentary contrasts a guided path with directionless loss; Proverbs describes those whose paths are crooked and ways devious.
The commentary says a path has an endpoint while dalal loses the destination; Proverbs warns that a way may seem right but its end is death.

row.basis: way of life and way of death
row.note: The commentary sets an arriving path against a lost way; Jeremiah explicitly places before the people a way of life and a way of death.

row.basis: walk in God's way and live
row.note: The commentary asks for guidance along the path of those favored; Deuteronomy links walking in God's ways with life and blessing.
The commentary contrasts a path that arrives with a lost way; Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses and urges Israel to choose life.

row.basis: they do not know the way of peace
row.note: The commentary's dalal is loss of direction; Isaiah says the people do not know the way of peace and have made their paths crooked.
The commentary says a traveler may leave sight yet still be carried toward an arrival; Isaiah recalls God making a road through the sea for Israel's passage.
The commentary's path has direction and destination; Isaiah promises a new way in the wilderness and water in the desert, turning a trackless place into a route.

row.basis: prepare a way in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary's sirat is a road that carries travelers toward an arrival; Isaiah calls for a way to be prepared in the wilderness for God's coming.

row.basis: Isaiah's road read as John's preparation
row.note: The commentary treats the straight path as a route of divine guidance; Mark applies Isaiah's wilderness-road language to John preparing Jesus' arrival, giving the road a Christian messianic reading.

row.basis: path of life in God's presence
row.note: The commentary says the sirat goes somewhere; the psalmist says God makes known the path of life, whose destination is joy in God's presence.

row.basis: word as lamp for the path
row.note: The commentary's blind travelers cannot see the way; the psalm calls God's word a lamp to the feet and light to the path, supplying the light they lack.
The commentary contrasts the guided path with dalal; Hosea's closing line says the Lord's ways are straight, the righteous walk in them, and transgressors stumble.

row.basis: guarding the going out and coming in
row.note: The commentary pictures a traveler who leaves sight but has a destination; the psalm's close asks God to guard the worshipper's going out and coming in continually.

row.basis: kept on the journey and brought back
row.note: The commentary says a path may hide the traveler while still reaching its end; God promises Jacob presence wherever he goes and return to the land.
The commentary's road has a destination; the Song of the Sea says God leads the redeemed people toward the dwelling of his holiness.

row.basis: walking in darkness without knowing where
row.note: The commentary uses dalal for one who goes where no one knows; Jesus warns that the one walking in darkness does not know where he is going.

row.basis: make straight paths so the lame may heal
row.note: The commentary requests a straight road; Hebrews urges straight paths for the feet so the impaired limb may be healed rather than further dislocated.
The commentary says a traveler can disappear from the observer's sight while continuing along a route; on the Emmaus road, the disciples walk with Jesus but their eyes are kept from recognizing him.

row.basis: recognition and disappearance at the destination
row.note: The commentary joins leaving sight with eventual arrival; at Emmaus the travelers recognize Jesus at the meal and he disappears from their sight, after the road has brought them to understanding.

row.basis: Philip directed onto a desert road
row.note: The commentary describes a traveler on a route with a destination; an angel sends Philip onto the Jerusalem-to-Gaza road, where the encounter that follows leads to the eunuch's baptism.
The commentary says a road has direction and destination; Paul's vision of a Macedonian asking for help redirects his travel toward a new destination.
The commentary says Joseph's disappearance in the pit leads into a travelers' route; Genesis gives that route an Egyptian destination when Joseph is sold to Potiphar.
The commentary reads Joseph's pit and sale as a journey with an eventual destination; the psalm retells the story as God sending Joseph ahead of his family.
The commentary says Joseph's disappearance leads into the road of travelers; Stephen's retelling continues with God delivering Joseph and making him ruler in Egypt.

row.basis: God chooses not to remember forgiven sin
row.note: The commentary says the Lord neither loses nor forgets; Jeremiah's new-covenant promise says God will forgive and remember sin no more, distinguishing deliberate pardon from loss of knowledge.

row.basis: Jeremiah's promise applied to the new covenant
row.note: The commentary's claim that God does not lose or forget meets Hebrews' quotation of Jeremiah that God will remember sins no more; Hebrews frames that promise as the new covenant established through Jesus.
The commentary says God's knowledge does not lose what is entrusted to it; Isaiah intensifies the promise not to forget Zion by picturing her inscribed on God's hands.

row.basis: Moses asks to be blotted from the book
row.note: The commentary says God keeps people from being lost in memory; Moses invokes God's book while offering himself for Israel, making inclusion in the divine record explicit.
The commentary says God neither loses nor forgets; God answers that the one who sins will be blotted from his book, adding accountability to the image of divine memory.

row.basis: written in the book and delivered
row.note: The commentary says none are lost from God's knowledge; Daniel says those found written in the book will be delivered at the time of distress.
The commentary says the Lord does not lose or forget; Jesus tells the disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven.
The commentary says God neither loses nor forgets; Paul says the Lord knows those who are his, marking divine recognition as secure.
The commentary gives a secondary sense of dalal as something vanishing from memory; Peter links short-sighted blindness with forgetting the cleansing from former sins.
The commentary says the fabricated objects disappear from their adherents; Paul says an idol is nothing in the world, recasting their failure as the absence of a true divine power.

row.basis: turn from idols to serve the living God
row.note: The commentary says fabricated objects leave their worshippers; Paul describes converts turning from idols to serve the living and true God.
The commentary says the day gathers people and no one is absent; Jesus depicts all nations gathered before the Son of Man and separated for judgment.
The commentary says nothing can be absent from the Day of Judgment; Jesus says people will answer for every careless word on that day.
The commentary denies that anyone or anything is missing from judgment; Paul says God judges people's secrets through Jesus Christ.
